definition: Some editors of Wikimedia projects use artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning programs to edit existing articles or create new ones.
details: Some applications of artificial intelligence, like using large language models (LLMs) to create new articles from scratch, have been more controversial than others for the Wikipedia community. In August 2025, English Wikipedia adopted a policy that allowed editors to nominate suspected LLM-generated articles for speedy deletion. This was followed by a March 2026 decision to prohibit the use of LLMs to generate or rewrite article content, with exceptions for copyediting one's own writing and machine translation from another language's Wikipedia. Wikipedia has also been a significant source of training data for some of the earliest artificial intelligence projects. This has received mixed reactions including concern about companies not citing Wikipedia when relying on it to answer a question as well as Wikipedia's increased costs from data scraping.

explainer.lead: Artificial intelligence is used both to help maintain Wikimedia projects and, more controversially, to write Wikipedia articles. At the same time, Wikipedia's text and discussions have become valuable training data for AI systems, creating disputes over reliability, attribution, and the cost of data scraping.

tiers.eli5: Wikipedia is like a huge shared school project, and some people bring in computer helpers to fix mistakes or write drafts. Those helpers can save time, but they can also confidently invent facts and references, so editors check their work and sometimes remove it. Wikipedia's pages also help teach AI programs about language.
tiers.practitioner: On Wikipedia, AI-related tools range from supervised bots and vandalism classifiers to LLM-assisted drafting and machine translation. Detection combines software, wiki-scripts, edit filters, paste warnings, and human review, with fabricated citations and unverifiable text among the main warning signs. English Wikipedia's March 2026 rule prohibits AI-generated article content except for copyediting and machine translation from another language's Wikipedia.
tiers.paperLevel: The term covers two reciprocal relationships: the application of AI and machine learning to editing Wikimedia projects, and the use of Wikimedia content as machine-learning data. Documented failure modes for LLM-assisted editing include plausible misinformation, fabricated references, non-encyclopedic prose, and reproduced biases. Large-scale reuse of Wikipedia also raises unresolved concerns about attribution and scraping costs.

explainer.example: On December 6, 2022, Richard Knipel used ChatGPT to draft the article "Artwork title." In another early experiment, ChatGPT produced a decent overview of "Weaponized incompetence" but fabricated its citations, illustrating why readable output does not establish reliability.

usedIn.name: ClueBot NG
usedIn.detail: Uses an artificial neural network to identify likely vandalism on Wikipedia.

usedIn.name: ORES
usedIn.detail: Aaron Halfaker's Objective Revision Evaluation Service, launched in late 2015 to grade Wikipedia edit quality.

usedIn.name: Google Perspective API
usedIn.detail: Its development used hundreds of thousands of Wikipedia talk-page comments with human-labelled toxicity levels.

usedIn.name: Large language model training
usedIn.detail: Wikipedia corpus subsets have served as large, well-curated training datasets.

explainer.intuition: Think of AI as both a fast but fallible editorial assistant and a student learning from Wikipedia. Automation can handle repetitive maintenance, while generated article text needs unusually careful checking because fluent writing can conceal false claims and sources.
howItWorks: Approved, human-supervised bots automate repetitive tasks such as creating short articles from structured data or fighting vandalism.
Machine-learning systems classify edits or content, including ClueBot NG's neural-network vandalism detection and ORES's edit-quality grading.
Editors may experiment with LLMs or machine translation, but generated claims and citations must be assessed against Wikipedia's content policies.
Specialized software, scripts, filters, paste warnings, and human judgment help identify suspected AI additions.
Separately, AI developers train systems on Wikipedia articles or labelled talk-page discussions.
explainer.whyItMatters: AI can reduce routine editorial work, but mass-produced misinformation shifts costly verification and cleanup onto volunteers. Wikipedia's use as training data also affects how AI systems answer questions and who bears the infrastructure costs of supplying that data.
misconceptions: AI on Wikipedia does not mean only ChatGPT: approved bots have operated there since 2002.
Fluent, Wikipedia-style prose is not evidence that an article's claims or references are genuine.
AI detection is not a single automated verdict; it combines tools with human review and writing clues.
